TP.sentence: A score of 0-13 results in a grade of A.
A score of 14-27 results in a grade of B.
A score of 28 or more results in a grade of C.
Every food service establishment is scheduled for at least one inspection per year.

FP.sentence: A restaurant may also be closed if it scores 28 or more points on three consecutive inspections.
After re-opening, the establishment will be inspected for compliance with the Health Code.

As of July 2010, certain types of food service establishments—including restaurants, coffee shops, bars, nightclubs and most cafeterias and fixed-site food stands—must post letter grades that correspond to their sanitary inspection scores.

Letter grades are not issued to mobile food vending units, temporary food service establishments, food service establishments operated by primary or secondary schools, hospital-operated cafeterias, correctional facilities, charitable organizations (including soup kitchens or other prepared food distribution programs) or food service establishments operated by not-for-profit membership organizations that serve food only to their members.
Only certain inspections result in a grade.
The frequency of inspections depends on a restaurant's score.
It must be on the front window, door or an outside-facing wall.
The card must be within 5 feet from the front door or other entrance, and within 6 feet from the ground or floor.

FN.sentence: A restaurant that scores 0 to 13 violations points on its first inspection will receive an A-grade card that must be posted immediately.
If an A is issued on re-inspection, the A-grade card must be posted immediately.
An establishment receiving a B or C grade on re-inspection receives two cards: one showing the letter grade and one that says "Grade Pending"; one of those cards must be posted immediately.

TN.sentence: The Health Department may order a restaurant to temporarily close to correct a public health hazard that cannot be corrected before the end of an inspection or when the restaurant is operating without a valid permit.
Prior to closure, an inspector will contact a supervisor, who will determine whether to order the establishment closed.

If it is closed, Health Department closure signs must be immediately posted in the window(s) and/or door(s), all operations must cease and the restaurant must remain closed for business until it is authorized by the Health Department to reopen.
The Department will monitor the establishment to ensure it remains closed and will issue additional violations for not complying with the closing order.
To reopen, the establishment must submit a written statement to the Health Department indicating that it has corrected all the violations that led to its being closed.
The operator may be asked to attend an informal meeting with Health Department supervisors.
If it appears that sanitary conditions have improved, an inspector will conduct a reopening inspection while the establishment remains closed to the public.
Health Department supervisors will determine whether it may reopen.
If it is in sufficient compliance, it may remain open and will be inspected again in about three months.
Repeated violations may prompt the Health Department to initiate procedures for the revocation or suspension of the operator's permit at a hearing before OATH.
